startup.name: Pagewise
startup.one_liner: An API that turns messy PDFs and scans into clean structured data for finance teams.
startup.description: ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE, not a real company. Pagewise sells a document extraction API to finance and operations teams. It reads invoices, statements and contracts, returns structured fields and flags low-confidence values for human review. Priced per page with a monthly minimum.

yc_acceptance.basis: Illustrative numbers, not calibrated. Start from a low single digit published acceptance rate, then adjust up for a crowded but clearly funded category with proven demand, and down for no stated traction or founder track record in the description.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC has funded several document AI companies already and recently. Without live customers or a sharp edge over them, the application reads as a thinner version of a company that is already ahead. The application would also need a concrete reason the team can win against companies that are already ahead and well funded.

killers.risk: Model vendors ship document extraction as a built in feature
killers.evidence: Large model providers already read PDFs and images in their base products, and the price per page is falling.
killers.mitigation: Own the review workflow and the integrations, not the extraction itself.

killers.risk: Customers will not pay more than a few cents a page
killers.evidence: Buyers compare per page prices openly and many try three vendors in a week.
killers.mitigation: Sell outcomes (closed books, audited fields) instead of pages.

killers.risk: Enterprise sales cycles outlast the seed money
killers.evidence: Finance buyers require security reviews and pilots that take months.
killers.mitigation: Start with mid sized teams that can buy within weeks.

killers.risk: Already funded category leaders pull ahead
killers.evidence: A document AI company in the same wedge raised a Series B only about a year after its seed.
killers.mitigation: Pick a vertical (for example construction invoices) where the leaders do not specialize.

killers.risk: Founders have no stated edge in finance workflows
killers.evidence: The description lists no customers, no pilots and no finance operating experience among the founders, so the team's edge is unproven.
killers.mitigation: Add a finance operator as a co-founder or design partner before applying.

technical_complexity.rationale: Extraction accuracy on messy documents is hard, but a small team can reach a useful level by combining existing models with checks and a review step. The hard part is long tail document types, not the first demo.

takeover_risk.rationale: Platforms already ship file reading and could add finance specific templates quickly. They lack the review workflow and integrations, which is where a startup can defend itself.

evidence.claim: Finance teams still key in invoices by hand at many mid sized companies.
Document AI is a funded category with several YC companies raising growth rounds.

pros.evidence: A direct comparable raised a seed, A and B quickly, so buyers and investors exist.
Per page pricing is easy to explain and to test with pilots.
Existing models plus a review step reach a useful product in about three months.

brand.rationale: The name is short, readable and fits a document product, but it sits among many similar compound names and gives the brand no obvious character. It will not hurt the company and will not help it stand out either. This is an illustrative judgment, not a researched one.

narrative.headline: Real demand, a crowded field, and most likely a stall around Seed unless it finds a vertical the leaders ignore.
narrative.general_summary: Pagewise sells document extraction to finance teams. The need is real and funded, and a close comparable raised three rounds quickly. That cuts both ways: the category is crowded and platforms are moving into it. If it is accepted into YC, the most likely path is a modest seed and a stall before Series A. The upside case needs a narrow vertical, a review workflow that customers rely on, and early enterprise logos. This is an illustrative example with hand set numbers, built to show the report format.
